Chapter 13: Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework

Data Science and Macroeconomic Models: A Python Companion to Intermediate Macroeconomics · Carlos Mendez

How to use this notebook. In Colab, click Runtime → Run all. After that, every model figure has live sliders: move one and the model is solved again on the spot. On the book website the same figures come with one precomputed slider. Each section ends with a short Your turn task, and you can try it in the empty code cell below the task.

Sources and credits. The figures are our own adaptations of, or are inspired by, the figures in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton. A Sources note below each figure names the original figure and links to the data, so you can explore the sources yourself.

Learning goals

Chapters 11 and 12 built the short-run model from three pieces: the IS curve, the MP curve and the Phillips curve. In those chapters the central bank chose the interest rate case by case. This chapter gives it a rule, and the whole short-run model then fits in one familiar diagram. By the end of it you will be able to:

  • combine the IS curve with a monetary policy rule to get the aggregate demand (AD) curve, and read the Phillips curve as an aggregate supply (AS) curve;
  • solve the AS/AD model for its steady state and for the path of inflation and output, period by period, after an inflation shock, a disinflation and an aggregate demand shock;
  • explain why expectations, credibility and inflation targets matter for the cost of fighting inflation;
  • test the model on U.S. data, and on data for dozens of other countries: policy rates against the policy rule, inflation-output loops, and three centuries of inflation;
  • in Python: write one simulate loop and reuse it in many figures, build tables from lists of dictionaries, reshape data with melt, join tables with merge, and compare two vintages of the same data.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

The model in code

The short-run model of Chapter 12 has three equations: the IS curve \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r})\), the MP curve (the central bank chooses \(R_t\)) and the Phillips curve \(\Delta\pi_t = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\). This chapter replaces the MP curve with a monetary policy rule: the central bank raises the real interest rate above the marginal product of capital whenever inflation is above its inflation target \(\bar{\pi}\),

\[R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \qquad (13.1)\]

The parameter \(\bar{m}\) says how hard the central bank leans against inflation. Substitute the rule into the IS curve and you get the AD curve. Write the Phillips curve in levels and you get the AS curve:

\[\text{AD:}\quad \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}), \qquad (13.3)\]

\[\text{AS:}\quad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}. \qquad (13.4)\]

Last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\) in the AS curve is expected inflation: firms expect inflation to stay where it was (adaptive expectations, \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\)). We write it as pi_e in the code, because Figure 20 will let expectations be formed differently.

The model has two unknowns, \(\tilde{Y}_t\) and \(\pi_t\). Substitute the AS curve into the AD curve and solve for output; then the AS curve gives inflation:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi^e_t + \bar{o} - \bar{\pi})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]

One baseline for every diagram. The textbook draws its diagrams without numbers. All the diagrams of this notebook start from one illustrative set of parameters:

  • inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent, the target of the U.S., the U.K., the euro area and Japan;
  • policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), John Taylor’s value, used again in Figure 16;
  • interest sensitivity \(\bar{b} = 2\), as in Chapter 11’s example;
  • Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\) (illustrative);
  • the shocks: an inflation shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) points for one period, an aggregate demand shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) points for nine periods, and a disinflation from a target of 4 to 2 percent (the numbers of textbook Figure 13.20).

With these values \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\), so the denominator above is 2: after any shock, the economy closes half of the remaining inflation gap every period. That matches the spacing of the textbook’s figures. \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{m}\) enter the dynamics only through their product, so the event figures have a slider for \(\bar{m}\) and keep \(\bar{b} = 2\).

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing m=M_BAR gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma.

PI_BAR, M_BAR, B_BAR, NU_BAR = 2.0, 0.5, 2.0, 1.0   # the baseline: target 2%, m = 1/2, b = 2, nu = 1
PI_OLD = 4.0                                         # the inflation target before the disinflation
A_LAST = 9                                           # the demand shock lasts from period 1 to period 9
T_MAX = 20                                           # number of periods simulated after each event


def ad_output(pi, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, a=0.0, b=B_BAR):
    """Equation 13.3, the AD curve: Y~ = a - b m (pi - pi_bar), in percent."""
    return a - b * m * (pi - pi_bar)


def as_inflation(Y, pi_e=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0):
    """Equation 13.4, the AS curve: pi = pi_e + nu Y~ + o, with expected inflation pi_e (= pi_{t-1})."""
    return pi_e + nu * Y + o


def solve_asad(pi_e, a=0.0, o=0.0, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The point where the AD and AS curves cross: short-run output and inflation in one period."""
    Y = (a - B_BAR * m * (pi_e + o - pi_bar)) / (1 + B_BAR * m * nu)
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu, o)

Let us try solve_asad on two cases: the steady state, and the first period of an inflation shock.

Python note. Y, pi = solve_asad(...) unpacks the two results into two variables. An f-string such as f"Y~ = {Y:.2f}" inserts a value into text; :.2f means “show two decimals”.

Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e=2.0)
print(f"Steady state (expected inflation = target = 2%):  Y~ = {Y:.2f}%,  pi = {pi:.2f}%")
Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e=2.0, o=2.0)
print(f"Inflation shock o = 2 hits the steady state:      Y~ = {Y:.2f}%,  pi = {pi:.2f}%")
Steady state (expected inflation = target = 2%):  Y~ = 0.00%,  pi = 2.00%
Inflation shock o = 2 hits the steady state:      Y~ = -1.00%,  pi = 3.00%

In the steady state output is at potential and inflation equals the target. The shock raises inflation by only 1 point, not 2, because the central bank answers with a recession of 1 percent.

One loop for every event

The events of this chapter play out over many periods. Each period, firms expect last period’s inflation, and the economy jumps to the point where that period’s AD and AS curves cross. simulate repeats this step period by period. It takes one list of demand shocks \(\bar{a}\) and one list of inflation shocks \(\bar{o}\), one value per period, and returns a table with one row per period. shock_list builds those lists.

Python note. values.append(x) adds x at the end of the list values, and for t in range(1, 21) repeats the indented lines for t = 1, 2, …, 20. dict(period=0, Y=0.0) is a dictionary: a set of named values. rows[-1] is the last element of a list, and rows[-1]["pi"] its value named "pi". pd.DataFrame(rows) turns a list of dictionaries into a table, one row per dictionary.

def shock_list(size, last):
    """A shock of the given size in periods 1, ..., last and zero afterwards, for T_MAX periods."""
    values = []
    for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1):
        if t <= last:
            values.append(size)
        else:
            values.append(0.0)
    return values


NO_SHOCK = shock_list(0.0, 0)                   # T_MAX zeros


def simulate(a_list, o_list, pi_start=PI_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Solve the AS/AD model period by period; period 0 is the old steady state with inflation pi_start."""
    rows = [dict(period=0, a=0.0, o=0.0, target=pi_start, pi_e=pi_start, Y=0.0, pi=pi_start)]
    for t in range(1, len(a_list) + 1):
        pi_e = rows[-1]["pi"]                   # adaptive expectations: last period's inflation
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a_list[t - 1], o_list[t - 1], pi_bar, m, nu)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, a=a_list[t - 1], o=o_list[t - 1], target=pi_bar, pi_e=pi_e, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(2.0, 1)).head(6).round(3)
period a o target pi_e Y pi
0 0 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.000 0.000 2.000
1 1 0.0 2.0 2.0 2.000 -1.000 3.000
2 2 0.0 0.0 2.0 3.000 -0.500 2.500
3 3 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.500 -0.250 2.250
4 4 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.250 -0.125 2.125
5 5 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.125 -0.062 2.062

The table is the inflation shock of Figures 6 to 9: inflation jumps to 3 percent in period 1, then falls to 2.5, 2.25, 2.125, …; the gap to the 2 percent target halves every period, and so does the recession. The column target is the inflation target behind each period’s AD curve, and pi_e is expected inflation, the height of that period’s AS curve at \(\tilde{Y} = 0\).

Drawing tools

Every diagram below uses the same axes and the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

  • add_ad and add_as draw one curve and write its name at its right end;
  • add_point marks a point with dashed guides to the axes, and add_arrow draws an arrow;
  • asad_figure starts a figure with one or two panels, and asad_axes fixes the axes and writes the title.

Python note. np.linspace(-15, 15, 241) creates 241 evenly spaced numbers from −15 to 15, one every 0.125. Because our model functions work on a whole array at once, one call gives a whole curve. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) creates a figure with two panels side by side, and add_trace(..., row=1, col=2) draws in the second panel. (x >= 0) & (y <= 8) is true where both conditions hold, x[inside] keeps the values where inside is true, and [-1] takes the last of them. Labels such as "AS<sub>2</sub>" use HTML to write AS₂. fig.data is the list of traces already drawn, min(a, b) and max(a, b) give the smaller and the larger of two numbers, and tickvals=None lets Plotly choose the tick marks itself. The axes stay fixed for every slider setting except a few extreme ones, where asad_axes widens them so that no dot falls off the chart. fig.update_annotations(yshift=16) moves every text already in the figure (here only the panel titles) 16 pixels up.

Y_GRID = np.linspace(-15, 15, 241)          # output levels at which we draw the AS curves
PI_GRID = np.linspace(12, -5, 137)          # inflation rates, high to low, at which we draw the AD curves
X_RANGE, PI_RANGE = [-4, 4], [-1, 8]        # fixed axes, so that you can see the curves move
FADED = "rgba(0,128,112,0.35)"              # light teal for the AS curves of earlier periods


def axis_names(col):
    """The names Plotly gives the axes of panel col: x and y in panel 1, x2 and y2 in panel 2."""
    if col == 1:
        return "x", "y"
    return f"x{col}", f"y{col}"


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw one curve in panel col and write its label at its last point inside the axes."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    inside = (x >= X_RANGE[0]) & (x <= X_RANGE[1]) & (y >= PI_RANGE[0]) & (y <= PI_RANGE[1])
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], xref=xref, yref=yref, text=label, showarrow=False,
                           xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))
def add_ad(fig, label, color, a=0.0, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, b=B_BAR, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw an AD curve (equation 13.3): output on the horizontal axis, inflation on the vertical axis."""
    add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_GRID, pi_bar, m, a, b), PI_GRID, label, color, dash, col)


def add_as(fig, label, color, pi_e=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw an AS curve (equation 13.4)."""
    add_curve(fig, Y_GRID, as_inflation(Y_GRID, pi_e, nu, o), label, color, dash, col)


def add_point(fig, Y, pi, label, col=1, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (Y, pi) with a dot and a label, and (if guides) dashed lines to both axes."""
    if guides:
        # the guides start far outside the chart: the axes cut them off at their edges, wherever these are
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[-100, Y, Y], y=[pi, pi, -100], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                                 hoverinfo="skip", line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[Y], y=[pi], mode="markers", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)
    if label != "":
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        # well above the dot and a little to the right: clear of the curves and the dashed guides through it
        fig.add_annotation(x=Y, y=pi, xref=xref, yref=yref, text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                           yanchor="bottom", xshift=4, yshift=8, font=dict(size=16))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, col=1):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; nothing if the two points almost coincide."""
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref=xref, yref=yref, axref=xref, ayref=yref, text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")
def asad_figure(cols=1, titles=None):
    """An empty figure with cols panels side by side (titles: one short title per panel)."""
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=cols, subplot_titles=titles, horizontal_spacing=0.1)
    fig.update_annotations(yshift=16)           # lift the panel titles clear of curve labels at the top edge
    return fig


def asad_axes(fig, title, panels=1):
    """Fixed AS/AD axes in the first panels (no tick in the bottom-left corner) and the title readout."""
    x_range, pi_range = list(X_RANGE), list(PI_RANGE)
    for trace in fig.data:                       # the dots: widen an axis only if a dot would fall off the chart
        if trace.mode == "markers":
            x_range = [min(x_range[0], trace.x[0] - 0.5), max(x_range[1], trace.x[0] + 0.5)]
            pi_range = [min(pi_range[0], trace.y[0] - 0.4), max(pi_range[1], trace.y[0] + 0.8)]
    x_ticks, pi_ticks = list(range(-3, 4)), list(range(0, 8))
    if x_range != X_RANGE or pi_range != PI_RANGE:
        x_ticks, pi_ticks = None, None           # wider axes: let Plotly choose the ticks
    for col in range(1, panels + 1):
        fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Output, Ỹ (percent)", range=x_range, tickvals=x_ticks, zeroline=False,
                         row=1, col=col)
        fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Inflation, π (percent)", range=pi_range, tickvals=pi_ticks, zeroline=False,
                         row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_layout(title=title, legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top",
                                               bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))

Countries and colors

The data figures at the end of this chapter (Figures 16–21) can go beyond the textbook’s economies: the same series exist for many other countries. The file countries.csv lists every economy in the chapter’s multi-country files, with its region and whether it belongs to the OECD. We give each country a fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others, and two countries that are shown together never share a color. The function missing_or_off writes a short note for a chart title when a chosen country has no data or leaves the chart.

Python note. PALETTE.index(c) finds the position of color c, .pop(i) removes the item at that position and returns it, and .append puts it at the end. group_colors walks through the countries one by one. colors.get(other) is the color of other, or None if it has none yet. new + free + PALETTE joins three lists and [0] takes the first item: a color that no country uses yet if there is one, else one that no country of the same groups uses.

LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]      # too pale on a white page
PALETTE = list(px.colors.qualitative.Dark24)                                     # 24 dark colors ...
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:                                     # ... and 20 more
    if color not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(color)
PALETTE.append(PALETTE.pop(PALETTE.index("#2E91E5")))   # this blue is close to the U.S. navy: move it to the end
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country of its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.
    groups: lists of countries shown together (the website menus); fixed: {country: color} for the book's countries."""
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        if name in colors:
            continue
        used = []                                    # colors of the countries already shown with this one
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    used.append(colors.get(other))
        free, new = [], []                           # free: not used in its groups; new: not used by any country
        for color in PALETTE:
            if color not in used:
                free.append(color)
                if color not in colors.values():
                    new.append(color)
        colors[name] = (new + free + PALETTE)[0]
    return colors

Python note. values.empty is true when a selection has no rows. ", ".join(names) glues a list of names into one text, with a comma between them.

def missing_or_off(part, column, countries, low, high):
    """Title text naming the chosen countries with no data in `part`, and those whose values leave [low, high]."""
    missing, off = [], []
    for name in countries:
        values = part[column][part.country == name]
        if values.empty:
            missing.append(name)
        elif values.min() < low or values.max() > high:
            off.append(name)
    note = ""
    if missing:
        note += "; no data: " + ", ".join(missing)
    if off:
        note += "; off the chart: " + ", ".join(off)
    return note

The website versions of the multi-country figures need two more helpers: a menu that switches between countries, and buttons that list one group of countries in the legend. Run the two cells and move on.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helpers for the website country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def compact(fig):
    """Shrink a website figure (short dates, 4 significant digits, a short hover), so the saved notebook stays small."""
    for trace in fig.data:
        x = pd.Series(trace.x if trace.x is not None else [], dtype=object).infer_objects()
        if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(x):
            trace.x = x.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist()
        if trace.y is not None and np.asarray(trace.y).dtype.kind == "f":
            trace.y = [float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in trace.y]
        if "lines" in (trace.mode or "") and trace.hovertext is None:
            trace.hovertemplate = "%{fullData.name}<br>%{x}: %{y}<extra></extra>"
    return fig


def menu_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one dropdown menu."""
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner, shown = [], []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            shown.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            trace.visible = shown[-1] if i == first else False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes], "legend.title.text": f.layout.legend.title.text,
                  "xaxis.range": f.layout.xaxis.range, "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range}
        visible = [shown[j] if o == i else False for j, o in enumerate(owner)]
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=110), updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=first, x=0, y=1.02,
                                                            xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])   # above the plot
    return compact(fig)
Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website group buttons (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def group_menu(fig, book, small=8):
    """Buttons that list one group of countries in the legend (a small group is drawn at once); `book` is always drawn."""
    names = [t.name for t in fig.data]
    short = {"Europe and Central Asia": "Europe", "Asia and Pacific": "Asia-Pacific", "Middle East and Africa": "Africa, Mideast"}
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Americas": [], "Europe": [], "Asia-Pacific": [], "Africa, Mideast": []}
    for c, r in zip(countries.country, countries.region):
        if c in names:
            groups[short.get(r, r)].append(c)
    first = ["legendonly" if len(names) <= 40 else False] * len(names)   # a short legend lists every country
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        if not set(members) & set(names):
            continue                                   # no country of this group in the figure
        visible = []
        for j, n in enumerate(names):
            if n in book:
                visible.append(True)
            elif n in members:
                visible.append(True if len(members) <= small else "legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(first[j] if label == "Textbook" else False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [dict(
        type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", buttons=buttons)])
    return compact(fig)

Figure 1: The aggregate demand curve

Goal. Build the AD curve from the IS curve and the policy rule, and see what each parameter does to it.

\[\left.\begin{array}{ll} \text{IS curve:} & \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r}) \\ \text{Policy rule:} & R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \end{array}\right\} \Rightarrow \text{AD curve: } \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\]

The AD curve slopes down, but not for the reason a demand curve for hamburgers does. It describes the central bank: when inflation is above target, the rule raises the real interest rate, investment falls, and output falls below potential. As with the IS curve, output goes on the horizontal axis.

The dot marks the point where inflation equals the target. There the interest-rate term is zero and output is \(\tilde{Y} = \bar{a}\): with no demand shock, potential output. When you change a parameter, the baseline curve stays behind as a dashed gray line.

Python note. if ... : runs the indented lines only when the condition is true. != means “is not equal to”, and comparing two groups of numbers in parentheses checks them all at once. x > 2.4 and y < 4.3 is true only when both conditions hold. We use it to leave out the baseline label when the new curve, or its own label, would run into it.

def ad_curve(pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, b=B_BAR, a=0.0):
    """Figure 13.1: the AD curve, with the point where inflation equals the target."""
    fig = asad_figure()
    if (pi_bar, m, b, a) != (PI_BAR, M_BAR, B_BAR, 0.0):
        label = "AD (baseline)"
        if ad_output(-1.0, pi_bar, m, a, b) > 2.4 and ad_output(-0.3, pi_bar, m, a, b) < 4.3:   # new AD too close
            label = ""
        add_ad(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, a, pi_bar, m, b)
    add_point(fig, a, pi_bar, "π = π̄")
    asad_axes(fig, f"AD: Ỹ = {a:.1f} − {b * m:.2f} × (π − {pi_bar:.1f});   at π = π̄ = {pi_bar:.1f}%, Ỹ = {a:.1f}%")
    return fig

Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

interact(ad_curve,
         pi_bar=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="inflation target π̄ (%)", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
         b=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.5, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="interest sensitivity b̄", style=WIDE),
         a=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-3.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="demand shock ā", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Figure 13.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton. Our own interactive version, with our own parameter values, layout and code; it is not a copy of the original figure.

What to notice.

  • The slope depends on the product \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\): each point of inflation above target costs \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 1\) point of output in the baseline. Raise \(\bar{m}\) or \(\bar{b}\) and the curve becomes flatter.
  • A demand shock \(\bar{a}\) and a new target \(\bar{\pi}\) shift the curve: \(\bar{a}\) moves it right or left, \(\bar{\pi}\) up or down. The dot always sits at \((\bar{a}, \bar{\pi})\).
  • A change in inflation itself does not shift the curve; it is a movement along it (Figure 2).

Your turn. The central bank raises its target from 2 to 3 percent. At an inflation rate of 3 percent, what output does the AD curve now give, compared with the baseline? Check with the sliders and with ad_output.

Hint

Compare ad_output(3.0) with ad_output(3.0, pi_bar=3.0). A higher target means the central bank sees less “excess” inflation at any given rate.

Figure 2: The AD curve after an inflation shock

Goal. See why higher inflation moves the economy along the AD curve instead of shifting it.

The economy starts in steady state at point \(A\): inflation at the 2 percent target, output at potential. Now inflation jumps to \(\pi' = 3\) percent. The policy rule raises the real interest rate by \(\bar{m}(\pi' - \bar{\pi}) = 0.5\) points, investment falls, and output falls to point \(B\). The readout in the title follows the chain: inflation, then the interest rate, then output. Figures 2 and 3 share one function.

def inflation_rises(pi_new=3.0, m=M_BAR):
    """Figures 13.2-13.3: inflation rises from the target to pi_new; the economy moves along AD from A to B."""
    Y_B = ad_output(pi_new, m=m)
    fig = asad_figure()
    if m != M_BAR:
        label = "AD (m̄ = 0.5)"
        if ad_output(-1.0, m=m) > 2.4 and ad_output(-0.3, m=m) < 4.3:   # the new AD would run into this label
            label = ""
        add_ad(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, m=m)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, PI_BAR, "A")
    if pi_new != PI_BAR:                                 # no second letter on top of A
        add_point(fig, Y_B, pi_new, "B")
    add_arrow(fig, -3.7, PI_BAR, -3.7, pi_new)      # inflation rises ...
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, -0.6, Y_B, -0.6)            # ... so output falls
    rate = m * (pi_new - PI_BAR)
    asad_axes(fig, f"π: {PI_BAR:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%   ⇒   R − r̄ = {rate:.2f}   ⇒   Ỹ: 0.00 → {Y_B:.2f}%")
    return fig
interact(inflation_rises,
         pi_new=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="new inflation rate π′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version

              label="new inflation rate π′ (%)")

Source. Adapted from Figure 13.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton. Our own interactive version, with our own parameter values, layout and code; it is not a copy of the original figure.

What to notice.

  • Only the point moves; the curve stays put. Inflation of 3 percent brings output to 1 percent below potential.
  • Move \(\pi'\) below 2 percent: the central bank cuts the real interest rate and output rises above potential.
  • The rule works through the real interest rate: \(R - \bar{r}\) in the title is the size of the policy response.

Key numbers: the policy rule

The textbook’s example: with \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), inflation 2 points above target raises the real interest rate by 1 point. Through the AD curve, that costs \(\bar{b} \times 1 = 2\) points of output.

Figure 3: An aggressive monetary policy rule

Goal. See how the policy response \(\bar{m}\) sets the slope of the AD curve.

A central bank with a high \(\bar{m}\) answers each point of extra inflation with a large rise in the real interest rate, and so with a deep recession. Its AD curve is flat: a small change in inflation means a big change in output. Here \(\bar{m} = 1\), twice the baseline, and the dashed gray line is the baseline AD curve. We keep the same rise in inflation as in Figure 2, so you can compare the two recessions.

Figure 4: The aggregate supply curve

Goal. Read the Phillips curve as an upward-sloping aggregate supply curve.

\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\]

At the start of period \(t\), last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\) is already known. So the Phillips curve is a relation between this year’s inflation and output. When output is above potential, firms work overtime to meet demand, and they raise their prices by more than usual to cover the extra costs: inflation rises. The curve crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at \(\pi_{t-1}\) (plus any inflation shock \(\bar{o}\)), so it shifts whenever inflation changes.

def as_curve(pi_prev=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0):
    """Figure 13.4: the AS curve, which crosses Y~ = 0 at last year's inflation plus the shock."""
    fig = asad_figure()
    if (pi_prev, nu, o) != (PI_BAR, NU_BAR, 0.0):
        label = "AS (baseline)"
        if abs(as_inflation(4.0, pi_prev, nu, o) - 6.0) < 0.6:   # the two labels at the right edge would overlap
            label = ""
        add_as(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    add_as(fig, "AS", TEAL, pi_prev, nu, o)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_prev + o, "")
    asad_axes(fig, f"AS: π = {pi_prev:.1f} + {nu:.2f} × Ỹ + {o:.1f};   at Ỹ = 0, π = {pi_prev + o:.1f}%")
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(r=120))               # room for the label "AS (baseline)" at the right edge
    return fig
interact(as_curve,
         pi_prev=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="last year's inflation π_{t−1} (%)",
                             style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="slope ν̄", style=WIDE),
         o=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=3.0, step=0.5, description="inflation shock ō", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

  • Last year’s inflation and the shock \(\bar{o}\) move the curve up and down, one for one.
  • \(\bar{\nu}\) turns the curve around the dot: a steeper curve means prices react more to a boom or a slump.
  • Because \(\pi_{t-1}\) is expected inflation, the AS curve carries expectations into the diagram. That is the key to every event below.

Figure 5: The AS/AD framework

Goal. Put the two curves in one diagram and find the short-run equilibrium, and the steady state.

This diagram is the whole short-run model: the inputs are the parameters (\(\bar{\pi}\), \(\bar{m}\), \(\bar{\nu}\)) and expected inflation, the outcomes are this period’s output and inflation. In a steady state inflation does not change, so \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1}\). The AS curve then requires \(\tilde{Y}^* = 0\), and the AD curve then requires \(\pi^* = \bar{\pi}\): inflation on target and output at potential. The readout tells you whether the crossing point is a steady state.

def asad_diagram(pi_e=PI_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figure 13.5: the AS and AD curves and the short-run equilibrium where they cross."""
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, pi_bar=pi_bar, m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_as(fig, "AS", TEAL, pi_e, nu)
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, pi_bar=pi_bar, m=m)
    add_point(fig, Y, pi, "")
    state = "the steady state"
    if pi_e != pi_bar:
        state = "not a steady state"
    asad_axes(fig, f"AS and AD cross at Ỹ = {Y:.2f}%, π = {pi:.2f}%: {state}")
    return fig
interact(asad_diagram,
         pi_e=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5, description="expected inflation π_{t−1} (%)",
                          style=WIDE),
         pi_bar=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.5, description="inflation target π̄ (%)", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="AS slope ν̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version

Source. Adapted from Figure 13.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton. Our own interactive version, with our own parameter values, layout and code; it is not a copy of the original figure.

What to notice.

  • When expected inflation equals the target, the curves cross at \((0, \bar{\pi})\) whatever \(\bar{m}\) and \(\bar{\nu}\) are.
  • Raise expected inflation to 4 percent: the AS curve shifts up, inflation rises and output falls. The crossing is not a steady state, because inflation will differ from what firms expected, and the AS curve will move again next period. The next figures follow that movement.
  • AD slopes down because of the central bank; AS slopes up because of firms’ pricing. Neither is a market demand or supply curve.

# Your turn: try it here

Figure 6: The initial response to an inflation shock

Goal. See the first period of Event #1: an inflation shock, such as a lasting rise in the price of oil.

The shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) hits for one period only. It shifts the AS curve up by 2 points, from AS to AS₁. If output stayed at potential, inflation would rise one for one, to 4 percent. But the policy rule fights the higher inflation with a higher interest rate, so the economy slides down the AD curve, from \(A\) to \(B\): inflation rises and output falls at the same time. This is stagflation, the U.S. experience after the oil shocks of the 1970s.

Figures 6 to 9 show the same event at different periods, so we write one function. It simulates the event with simulate and draws period t: the AS curves of the earlier periods in light teal, the current one in full color, and the path so far, with the textbook’s letters (\(B\), \(C\), \(D\) for periods 1, 2, 3).

Python note. path.loc[t] is the row of period t, and now.pi is its value in the column pi. path.pi_e[s] is the value of column pi_e in the row of period s. x in some_list is true when x is one of the elements, and "AD" if s == 0 else "AD₁" picks the first value when the condition holds, the second otherwise. round(x, 2) + 0.0 rounds to two decimals; adding 0.0 turns a rounded −0.0 into 0.0, so a title never shows “−0.00”.

def add_event_curves(fig, path, t, as_periods, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, col=1):
    """Curves of a simulated event at period t: the old AS, the AS of as_periods (the last one solid), every AD."""
    first, last = path.pi_e[0], as_periods[-1]
    today = path.pi_e[last] + path.o[last]                   # where today's AS crosses Y~ = 0
    near = 0.6 * max(1, nu)          # two AS labels closer than this would overlap (a steep AS exits at the top)
    same = today == first
    old_label = "AS" if same or abs(today - first) > near else ""     # no label on top of today's label
    add_as(fig, old_label, TEAL if same else GRAY, first, nu, dash="solid" if same else "dash", col=col)
    for s in as_periods:
        start = path.pi_e[s] + path.o[s]
        if start != first:                                   # skip curves that equal the original AS
            label = f"AS<sub>{s}</sub>" if s == last or (s == as_periods[0] and abs(start - today) > near) else ""
            add_as(fig, label, TEAL if s == last else FADED, path.pi_e[s], nu, path.o[s], col=col)
    drawn = []                                               # the AD curves already drawn: (a, target)
    for s in range(t + 1):
        pair = (path.a[s], path.target[s])
        if pair not in drawn:
            drawn.append(pair)
            name = "AD" if s == 0 else f"AD<sub>{s}</sub>"
            shift = abs(pair[0] - path.a[t] + B_BAR * m * (pair[1] - path.target[t]))   # 0 for today's AD
            if 0 < shift * min(1, 1 / (B_BAR * m)) < 0.6:          # an old label would sit on today's label
                name = ""
            add_ad(fig, name, BLUE if shift == 0 else GRAY, pair[0], pair[1], m,      # today's AD in blue
                   dash="solid" if shift == 0 else "dash", col=col)
def add_event_path(fig, path, t, letters, col=1):
    """The economy's path from A (period 0) to period t: dots, arrows, and the textbook's letters."""
    add_point(fig, path.Y[0], path.pi[0], "A", col)
    for s in range(1, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s], col)
        moved = (path.Y[s], path.pi[s]) != (path.Y[0], path.pi[0])   # with no shock, no letter on top of A
        if s in letters and moved:
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], letters[s], col)
        else:
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], "", col, guides=False)


SHOCK_LETTERS = {1: "B", 2: "C", 3: "D"}                     # the textbook's letters for periods 1-3


def inflation_shock(o=2.0, t=1, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figures 13.6 and 13.8: the economy t periods after a one-period inflation shock o."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(o, 1), m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_event_curves(fig, path, t, list(range(1, t + 1)), m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, t, SHOCK_LETTERS)
    now = path.loc[t]
    asad_axes(fig, f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:.2f}%   (shock ō = {o:.1f} in period 1 only)")
    return fig

What to notice.

  • The shock of 2 points raises inflation by only 1 point, to 3 percent, because output falls by 1 percent. Half of the shock shows up as inflation, half as recession, since \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\).
  • Raise \(\bar{m}\): the central bank fights harder, so inflation rises less and the recession is deeper.
  • A negative \(\bar{o}\) (say, a fall in oil prices) gives the mirror image: lower inflation and a boom.

Figure 7: Two periods after an inflation shock

Goal. See why the AS curve does not jump back after the shock ends.

In period 2 the shock is over, \(\bar{o} = 0\). But firms now expect last period’s inflation, \(\pi_1 = 3\) percent. So the new curve AS₂ crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at \(\pi_1\), above the original AS (panel a). High inflation raised expected inflation, and expectations adjust only slowly: inflation is sticky. In panel (b) the economy moves from \(B\) to \(C\): inflation falls a little, and the central bank lets output recover a little, though it stays below potential.

Python note. for col in [1, 2]: draws the same curves in both panels.

def two_periods(o=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figure 13.7: (a) the AS curve of period 2 and (b) the move from B to C."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(o, 1), m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = asad_figure(2, ("(a) Period 2: the AS curve moves to AS<sub>2</sub>", "(b) Period 2: the Fed steers the economy to C"))
    for col in [1, 2]:
        add_event_curves(fig, path, 2, [1, 2], m, nu, col)
    add_event_path(fig, path, 1, SHOCK_LETTERS, col=1)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, path.pi[1], "", col=1)               # AS2 crosses Y~ = 0 at pi_1
    add_event_path(fig, path, 2, SHOCK_LETTERS, col=2)
    now = path.loc[2]
    asad_axes(fig, f"Period 2: AS₂ starts from π₁ = {path.pi[1]:.2f}%; C: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {now.Y:.2f}%",
              panels=2)
    return fig

What to notice.

  • AS₂ lies between the original AS and AS₁: the shock is gone, but expected inflation is still 3 percent.
  • At \(C\) inflation is 2.5 percent and output is −0.5 percent: both gaps are half of what they were at \(B\).
  • The economy improves, but slowly. The same sticky expectations that keep inflation high keep the economy in a slump.

Figure 9: The effects of an inflation shock: summary

Goal. See the whole event at once, in the AS/AD diagram and over time.

Panel (a) is the textbook’s summary: the jump from \(A\) to \(B\), then the slow return along the AD curve back to \(A\). Panel (b) adds the same path as two time series, so you can read how long the stagflation lasts. One function draws the summaries of all three events (Figures 9, 11 and 15).

def add_time_paths(fig, path, col=2):
    """Inflation and output over time, with the inflation target, in panel col."""
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=path.period, y=path.pi, name="Inflation π", mode="lines+markers",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=path.period, y=path.Y, name="Output Ỹ", mode="lines+markers",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, T_MAX], y=[path.target[1], path.target[1]], name="Target π̄", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dot")), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Period", range=[-0.5, T_MAX + 0.5], tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20], row=1, col=col)
    low = min(-3, path.Y.min() - 0.5, path.pi.min() - 0.5)     # wider than -3 to 7 only if a path would leave it
    high = max(7, path.pi.max() + 0.5)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Percent", range=[low, high], tickvals=list(range(-12, 14, 2)), row=1, col=col)


def event_summary(path, letters, as_periods, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figures 13.9, 13.11, 13.15: (a) the whole path in the AS/AD diagram, (b) the same path over time."""
    fig = asad_figure(2, ("(a) The AS/AD diagram", "(b) Inflation and output over time"))
    add_event_curves(fig, path, T_MAX, as_periods, m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, T_MAX, letters)
    add_time_paths(fig, path)
    return fig


def inflation_shock_summary(o=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figure 13.9: a one-period inflation shock o, from the jump to B back to the steady state A."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(o, 1), m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = event_summary(path, {1: "B"}, [1], m, nu)
    asad_axes(fig, f"Shock ō = {o:.1f}: inflation peaks at {path.pi.max():.2f}%; sum of Ỹ = {round(path.Y.sum(), 2) + 0.0:.2f}")
    return fig

What to notice.

  • The shock lasts one period, but inflation stays above target for many periods, and output stays below potential all that time. Price shocks are insidious because they raise expected inflation.
  • The sum of output over all periods is −2.00: the total recession needed to undo the shock. A flatter AS curve (smaller \(\bar{\nu}\)) makes it longer and costlier, because prices then react less to a slump.
  • Change \(\bar{m}\): the recession becomes deeper but shorter, and the sum of output barely moves.

Key numbers: the inflation gap halves every period

With \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\), the AS/AD solution makes the gap between inflation and the target shrink by the factor \(1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) = 1/2\) each period.

path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(2.0, 1))
path["gap"] = path.pi - PI_BAR                   # inflation minus the target
path["gap ratio"] = path.gap / path.gap.shift(1)  # this period's gap divided by last period's
path.loc[0:6, ["period", "Y", "pi", "gap", "gap ratio"]].round(3)

0 0 0.000 2.000 0.000 NaN

Python note. path.gap.shift(1) moves the column down by one row, so each row sees last period’s gap. path.loc[0:6, [...]] keeps rows 0 to 6 and the listed columns.

From period 2 on the ratio is exactly 0.5. (Period 0 has no gap, so the ratio of period 1 divides by zero and pandas shows inf.) Inflation is 3, 2.5, 2.25, … and output −1, −0.5, −0.25, …

# Your turn: try it here

Figure 10: The initial response to disinflation

Goal. See Event #2: the central bank lowers its inflation target, as Paul Volcker’s Fed did in the 1980s.

The economy starts in a steady state with a target, and inflation, of 4 percent. The central bank now adopts a new rule with the target \(\bar{\pi}' = 2\) percent. The target appears only in the AD curve, so AD shifts down to AD₁: at any inflation rate the new rule wants lower output. Inflation of 4 percent is now “too high”, the real interest rate rises, and the economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\). The function reuses add_event_curves and add_event_path: only the event changes.

def disinflation(pi_new=2.0, t=1, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figures 13.10-13.11: t periods after the inflation target is cut from PI_OLD to pi_new."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, pi_new, m, nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_event_curves(fig, path, t, list(range(1, t + 1)), m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, t, {1: "B"})
    if t > 1:
        add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_new, "C")                     # the new steady state
    now = path.loc[t]
    asad_axes(fig, f"Target {PI_OLD:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%.  Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0:.2f}%")
    return fig

         pi_new=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="new target π̄′ (%)", style=WIDE),

         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="AS slope ν̄", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

  • Cutting the target by 2 points shifts AD down by exactly 2 points: AD₁ crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at the new target.
  • In period 1, inflation falls only to 3 percent, halfway between the old and the new target, and output falls 1 percent below potential.
  • The AS curve has not moved yet: firms still expect 4 percent inflation. Move the period slider to see it shift.

Figure 11: The dynamics of disinflation

Goal. Follow the disinflation to the new steady state \(C\).

After period 1, firms expect lower inflation, so the AS curve shifts down period by period, just as after the inflation shock. The economy slides down AD₁ from \(B\) to the new steady state \(C\), where inflation equals the new target and output is back at potential. The summary function of Figure 9 draws it; we add the point \(C\).

def disinflation_summary(pi_new=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figure 13.11: from A through B to the new steady state C, in the diagram and over time."""
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, pi_new, m, nu)
    fig = event_summary(path, {1: "B"}, [T_MAX], m, nu)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_new, "C")
    asad_axes(fig, f"Target {PI_OLD:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%: output lost over {T_MAX} periods = {round(-path.Y.sum(), 2) + 0.0:.2f}%")
    return fig

What to notice.

  • Inflation falls for good, from 4 to 2 percent, and output returns to potential. The price is a recession: about 2 percent of a year’s output in total.
  • A more aggressive central bank (higher \(\bar{m}\)) makes the recession deeper and shorter, but the total loss stays near 2. Only the AS slope \(\bar{\nu}\) changes it: the total loss is \((\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')/\bar{\nu}\).
  • Why must there be a recession at all? Because firms keep expecting the old inflation. If everyone believed the new target at once, the economy could jump straight from \(A\) to \(C\). Figure 20 returns to this idea.

Figure 13: Dynamics as the AS curve shifts

Goal. See that while the demand shock lasts, the economy drifts to higher inflation, not back to \(A\).

Inflation at \(B\) is above the 2 percent firms expected, so next period they expect 3 percent, and the AS curve shifts up. Period by period, inflation rises and output falls back toward zero, along AD₁. At \(C\) (period 8 in the textbook) output is back at potential, but inflation is well above target. There \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) on AD₁, so

\[0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi^c - \bar{\pi}) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \pi^c = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}.\]

It is the same demand_shock function, now at \(t = 8\).

Simulated output in period 8: 0.008%

Inflation approaches \(\pi^c = 4\) percent; after eight periods it is 3.992 percent and output is 0.008 percent. The textbook’s label “eight periods” is arbitrary: the economy gets close to \(C\) and never quite reaches it.

Your turn. Compute \(\pi^c\) for a central bank with \(\bar{m} = 1\), and check it against period 12 of a simulation with m=1.0.

Hint

The formula gives \(2 + 2/(2 \times 1)\). For the simulation, simulate(shock_list(2.0, A_LAST), NO_SHOCK, m=1.0).pi[...].

Figure 14: The unraveling after the aggregate demand shock ends

Goal. See what happens when the boom ends: a recession.

Demand shocks are temporary: in the long run \(\bar{a} = 0\), because the shares of output must add up to 1. When the European boom ends after period 9, the AD curve shifts back to its original position. Output was already at potential, so this works like a negative shock: the economy jumps from \(C\) to \(D\), below potential. The recession then pulls inflation down, the AS curve shifts down period by period, and the economy slides down the original AD curve back to \(A\). Again the same function, now at \(t = 10\).

What to notice.

  • At \(D\) inflation is 3 percent, the same as at \(B\), but output is 1 percent below potential. The textbook labels this \(\pi_1 = \pi_{10}\); it holds here because \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\).
  • From \(D\) the economy returns to \(A\) exactly as after the inflation shock: inflation and the recession halve each period.
  • Booms are matched by recessions: the inflation created by the boom can only be removed by a slump.

# Your turn: try it here

Figure 15: A positive aggregate demand shock: summary

Goal. See the whole boom-and-bust cycle, and what happens if the shock ends sooner.

The economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\), drifts to \(C\), jumps to \(D\) when the shock ends, and returns to \(A\): a counterclockwise loop. The textbook lets the economy reach \(C\) before the boom ends, but the boom could end sooner. The slider sets the last period of the shock; the letters \(C\) and \(D\) mark that period and the next one.

def demand_shock_summary(a=2.0, last=A_LAST, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figure 13.15: a demand shock a in periods 1 to last, in the AS/AD diagram and over time."""
    path = simulate(shock_list(a, last), NO_SHOCK, m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = event_summary(path, {1: "B", last: "C", last + 1: "D"}, [last], m, nu)
    asad_axes(fig, f"ā = {a:.1f} in periods 1–{last}: π peaks at {path.pi.max():.2f}%; sum of Ỹ = {round(path.Y.sum(), 2) + 0.0:.2f}")
    return fig

         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="AS slope ν̄", style=WIDE));

Source. Adapted from Figure 13.15 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton. Our own interactive version, with our own parameter values, layout and code; it is not a copy of the original figure.

What to notice.

  • The path runs counterclockwise: up and to the right (boom, rising inflation), up and to the left, then down and to the left (recession, falling inflation), and back.
  • The sum of output over the whole cycle is about zero: the boom and the recession cancel out. What remains is a long period of high inflation, a net cost. That is why central banks try to stabilize output.
  • End the shock early (2 or 3 periods): the loop is smaller, and inflation peaks lower.

# Your turn: try it here

Figure 16: The fed funds rate, actual and predicted

Goal. Test the policy rule on U.S. data: does it predict the Federal Reserve’s interest rate?

The rule sets the real interest rate, but the Fed sets a nominal rate, the fed funds rate. The Fisher equation links the two, \(i_t = R_t + \pi_t\), so the rule implies

\[i_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}). \qquad (13.5)\]

John Taylor picked numbers that are all built on the number 2: \(\bar{r} = 2\%\), \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and \(\bar{\pi} = 2\%\). Then \(i_t = 1 + 1.5\,\pi_t\): when inflation rises by 1 point, the nominal rate rises by 1.5 points, so the real rate rises too. For inflation we use core PCE inflation (prices of consumer spending without food and energy), the measure that reproduces the textbook’s line.

Python note. pd.read_csv reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns, and parse_dates=["date"] turns text such as "1960-01-01" into real dates. .tail() shows the last five rows.

taylor = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "taylor_rule.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
taylor.tail()
date fed_funds core_inflation
262 2025-07-01 4.2933 2.8371
263 2025-10-01 3.8967 2.7661
264 2026-01-01 3.6400 3.0012
265 2026-04-01 3.6333 3.0956
266 2026-07-01 3.6700 NaN

Each row is a quarter. fed_funds is the average fed funds rate in the quarter, and core_inflation is the core PCE inflation rate over the last four quarters, both in percent. The last row has no inflation yet: the data for that quarter were not published when the file was made. The rule will simply stop one quarter earlier.

The same test works for other central banks. The file taylor_rule_countries.csv has, for 33 economies, the quarterly average of the central bank’s policy rate (from the Bank for International Settlements) and core inflation, the consumer price index without food and energy (from the OECD). For the United States it repeats the table above.

rules = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "taylor_rule_countries.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
rules.dropna().groupby("country").date.agg(["min", "max"]).head(8)      # quarters with both series
min max
country
Australia 1976-07-01 2026-04-01
Austria 1967-01-01 1998-10-01
Belgium 1976-07-01 1998-10-01
Canada 1962-01-01 2025-01-01
Chile 1999-01-01 2023-10-01
Colombia 1996-01-01 2026-07-01

Look at your data. The coverage differs a lot. Germany, France, Italy and the other early euro members have their own policy rate only until 1998, and the euro area from 1999; core inflation starts in the 1970s or 1990s in many countries, and for Japan it stops in mid-2021. Israel and Mexico in the 1980s and Türkiye in the 1990s and 2020s had very high inflation, so the rule asks for rates far off the chart.

Python note. px.line with a list y=[...] draws one line per column. selector=dict(name=...) changes only the trace with that name. round(gap, 2) + 0.0 turns a rounded −0.00 into 0.00, and np.isnan(gap) is true when there were no quarters to average.

def policy_rule(pi, r_bar=2.0, m=M_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR):
    """Equation 13.5: the nominal interest rate i = r_bar + pi + m (pi - pi_bar)."""
    return r_bar + pi + m * (pi - pi_bar)
def fed_funds_chart(r_bar=2.0, m=M_BAR, country="United States"):
    """Figure 13.16: the actual policy rate of one country and the rate predicted by the policy rule."""
    part = rules[rules.country == country]
    actual = "Actual fed funds rate" if country == "United States" else "Actual policy rate"
    chart = pd.DataFrame({"date": part.date, actual: part.policy_rate,
                          "Policy rule": policy_rule(part.core_inflation, r_bar, m)})
    gap = round((chart[actual] - chart["Policy rule"])[chart.date >= "2009-01-01"].mean(), 2) + 0.0
    lines = chart[[actual, "Policy rule"]]
    low, high, ticks = -1, 22, [0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20]
    for wider_low, wider_high, wider_ticks in [(-5, 45, None), (-10, 110, None)]:   # only when a country needs it
        if lines.min().min() < low or lines.max().max() > high:
            low, high, ticks = wider_low, wider_high, wider_ticks
    title = f"Rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}, m̄ = {m:.2f}: actual minus rule since 2009 = {gap:.2f} points"
    if np.isnan(gap):
        title = f"Rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}, m̄ = {m:.2f} (no data since 2009)"
    legend = country + (" (off the chart)" if lines.min().min() < low or lines.max().max() > high else "")
    fig = px.line(chart, x="date", y=[actual, "Policy rule"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN], title=title,
                  labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=2.5)
    fig.update_traces(line_dash="dash", selector=dict(name="Policy rule"))
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=["1958-01-01", "2027-12-31"], yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=ticks),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text=legend)
    return fig

         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.0, max=1.0, step=0.25, description="m̄ in the rule", style=WIDE),
         country=Dropdown(options=sorted(rules.country.unique()), value="United States", description="country",
                          style=WIDE));

Sources. Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (FEDFUNDS), via FRED; U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, PCE price index excluding food and energy (JCXFE), via FRED; for the other economies, Bank for International Settlements, central bank policy rates (WS_CBPOL) and OECD, Consumer price indices, CPI excluding food and energy (DSD_PRICES@DF_PRICES_ALL), via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared files: data/ch13/taylor_rule.csv and data/ch13/taylor_rule_countries.csv (see the data notes). Figure: inspired by Figure 13.16 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton; our own chart, built from updated data.

On the website, the second chart offers the 33 economies, with Taylor’s numbers r̄ = 2 and m̄ = 1/2.

What to notice.

  • The simple rule follows the big swings of the actual rate surprisingly well: the rise in the 1970s, the peak around 1980, and the long decline afterward.
  • From the late 1960s to 1980 the actual rate was well below the rule: monetary policy was too loose, and inflation rose through the 1970s.
  • In recessions (early 1990s, early 2000s and above all after 2008) the Fed set rates far below the rule. The full Taylor rule also responds to output, which explains part of this.
  • Lower \(\bar{r}\) to 1 or 0.5 percent, as many economists now do: the rule comes closer after 2008, but in 2021–2022 it still calls for rates far above the actual ones. The Fed raised rates late after the Covid-19 pandemic.
  • Choose the euro area, the United Kingdom or Canada: the same pattern. Their central banks also kept rates below the rule after 2009 (by 2.2, 3.3 and 2.6 points on average from 2009 to 2020) and even more in 2021–2022 (by 4.7, 5.9 and 5.5 points). The rule uses core consumer prices for them, not the core PCE index of the U.S. line.

Key numbers: how closely does the Fed follow the rule?

Python note. taylor[(taylor.date >= start) & (taylor.date <= end)] keeps the quarters between two dates. .corr() gives the correlation between two columns: 1 means they move perfectly together. idxmax() gives the row number of the largest value, and :%Y-%m in an f-string writes a date as year-month.

taylor["rule"] = policy_rule(taylor.core_inflation)
taylor["gap"] = taylor.fed_funds - taylor.rule
for start, end in [("1967", "1980-12-31"), ("1990", "1993-12-31"), ("2001", "2004-12-31"),
                   ("2009", "2020-12-31"), ("2021", "2022-12-31")]:
    part = taylor[(taylor.date >= start) & (taylor.date <= end)]
    print(f"{start}-{end[:4]}: actual minus rule = {part.gap.mean():+.2f} points on average")
book_span = taylor[taylor.date <= "2023-01-01"]
print(f"Correlation of the actual rate with the rule, 1960Q1-2023Q1: {book_span.fed_funds.corr(book_span.rule):.2f}")
print(f"Highest rule rate: {taylor.rule.max():.2f}% in {taylor.date[taylor.rule.idxmax()]:%Y-%m}")
1967-1980: actual minus rule = -2.29 points on average
1990-1993: actual minus rule = -0.94 points on average
2001-2004: actual minus rule = -1.67 points on average
2009-2020: actual minus rule = -2.71 points on average
2021-2022: actual minus rule = -6.74 points on average
Correlation of the actual rate with the rule, 1960Q1-2023Q1: 0.75
Highest rule rate: 16.15% in 1975-01

The actual rate was below the rule by 2.3 points on average from 1967 to 1980, by 2.7 points from 2009 to 2020, and by 6.7 points in 2021–2022. The correlation of 0.75 says the two lines move together most of the time.

# Your turn: try it here

Figure 17: Inflation-output loops in the U.S. economy

Goal. Look for the model’s counterclockwise loops in U.S. data.

The model predicts that the economy moves in counterclockwise loops in a diagram with output on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis (Figure 15): a boom raises inflation, high inflation leads the central bank to cause a recession, and the recession brings inflation down. Each point below is one year: the output gap \(\tilde{Y}\) (actual GDP relative to the Congressional Budget Office’s estimate of potential GDP) and CPI inflation.

loops = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "loops_vintages.csv")
loops[loops.year.isin([2009, 2021, 2022, 2025])]
year inflation output_gap output_gap_2023
49 2009 -0.3204 -4.6619 -5.2000
61 2021 4.6812 0.8132 -1.2862
62 2022 7.9908 0.9160 -1.0390
65 2025 2.7058 1.3961 NaN

There are two output-gap columns. output_gap uses today’s data; output_gap_2023 uses the data as they were published in March 2023, when the textbook was written. GDP and, above all, the CBO’s potential GDP get revised: today’s estimate of potential output for 2021 is lower, so the same year now looks like a small boom (+0.8 percent) instead of a slump (−1.3 percent). The textbook’s data stop in 2022, so output_gap_2023 is empty (NaN) after that. Always check which vintage of the data a claim is based on.

Python note. .isin([...]) is true for the rows whose value is in the list. A dictionary such as WINDOWS maps a name to its settings, and WINDOWS[years] looks them up. .where(condition, "") keeps a value where the condition is true and puts an empty text elsewhere: we label only a few key years and let hover show the rest. .astype(str) turns the years into text. part.assign(label=...) returns a copy of the table with the new column label. MOVED.get(year, "top center") looks up year in the dictionary MOVED and gives "top center" when the year is not in it.

WINDOWS = {"1960–1985": (1960, 1985, [-8, 7], [0, 15], [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]),
           "1985–2025": (1985, 2025, [-6, 3], [-1.5, 9], [0, 2, 4, 6, 8])}
VINTAGES = {"Current data": "output_gap", "Textbook data": "output_gap_2023"}   # the textbook used the March 2023 vintage
KEY_YEARS = [1960, 1966, 1969, 1974, 1975, 1979, 1980, 1982, 1985, 1989, 1991, 2000, 2009, 2011, 2015,
             2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2025]
MOVED = {2020: "bottom center", 2021: "middle right", 2025: "bottom center"}   # labels moved off nearby points


def loops_chart(years="1960–1985", vintage="Current data"):
    """Figure 13.17: annual (output gap, inflation) points connected in time order."""
    first, last, x_range, y_range, y_ticks = WINDOWS[years]
    column = VINTAGES[vintage]
    part = loops[(loops.year >= first) & (loops.year <= last)].dropna(subset=[column])
    part = part.assign(label=part.year.astype(str).where(part.year.isin(KEY_YEARS), ""))
    fig = px.line(part, x=column, y="inflation", text="label", markers=True, hover_name="year",
                  labels={column: "Output gap, Ỹ (percent)", "inflation": "CPI inflation (percent)"},
                  title=f"Counterclockwise loops, {first}–{part.year.max()} ({vintage.lower()})")
    positions = []
    for year in part.year:
        positions.append(MOVED.get(year, "top center"))
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2), marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=7), textposition=positions)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis=dict(range=x_range, zeroline=True), yaxis=dict(range=y_range, tickvals=y_ticks))
    return fig

Python note. ToggleButtons shows one button per option, and the function receives the text of the chosen button.

interact(loops_chart,
         years=ToggleButtons(options=list(WINDOWS), value="1960–1985", description="years"),
         vintage=ToggleButtons(options=list(VINTAGES), value="Current data", description="data"));

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPC1), via FRED; Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential Gross Domestic Product (GDPPOT), via FRED; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPIAUCSL), via FRED; the textbook vintage of GDP and potential GDP (30 March 2023) from ALFRED, the St. Louis Fed’s archive of past data vintages. Prepared file: data/ch13/loops_vintages.csv (see the data notes). Figure: inspired by Figure 13.17 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton; our own chart, built from updated data.

What to notice.

  • Follow the years in 1960–1985: the boom of the late 1960s raises inflation, the high inflation of 1974–75 and 1979–80 is followed by deep recessions (1975, 1982), and inflation falls. The loops run counterclockwise, as the model predicts.
  • After 1985 the loops are smaller: the Great Moderation. The big exceptions are the deep slump of 2009–2011, during which inflation rose instead of falling, and the jump to 8 percent inflation in 2022.
  • Switch to the textbook data: the whole 1985–2022 cloud moves left by about 1 point. The shape of the loops is the same, but statements about the level of the gap depend on the vintage.

Key numbers: two vintages of the same year

The textbook says that in 2009 “output was more than 5 percent below potential”, and that inflation rose from 2009 to 2011 despite the slump.

Python note. .set_index("year") labels the rows by year, so by_year.loc[2009, "inflation"] picks one value.

by_year = loops.set_index("year")
print(f"2009 output gap: {by_year.loc[2009, 'output_gap_2023']:.2f}% (textbook data), "
      f"{by_year.loc[2009, 'output_gap']:.2f}% (current data)")
print(f"Inflation 2009 -> 2011: {by_year.loc[2009, 'inflation']:.2f}% -> {by_year.loc[2011, 'inflation']:.2f}%")
revision = (loops.output_gap - loops.output_gap_2023)[loops.year >= 1985]
print(f"Current minus textbook output gap, 1985-2022: {revision.mean():.2f} points on average, {revision.max():.2f} at most")
2009 output gap: -5.20% (textbook data), -4.66% (current data)
Inflation 2009 -> 2011: -0.32% -> 3.14%
Current minus textbook output gap, 1985-2022: 1.03 points on average, 2.10 at most

With the textbook’s data the 2009 gap is −5.20 percent; with today’s data it is −4.66 percent, so “more than 5 percent” is no longer true. Inflation did rise, from −0.32 to 3.14 percent, partly because of energy and commodity prices.

Loops in other countries

The OECD estimates the output gap of 40 economies, most of them since 1985, with one method for all. The file output_gaps_oecd.csv has these estimates, and inflation_annual.csv has CPI inflation for 194 economies (the World Bank’s numbers, and for the four economies of Figure 19 the numbers of that figure). We join them by country and year. For the United States the OECD’s gap differs from the CBO’s: it is 0.2 points higher on average since 1985, and −3.98 percent in 2009 instead of −4.66. Potential output cannot be observed, so every estimate of the gap is a model.

Python note. merge joins two tables on the columns they share, here iso3, country and year, and keeps the rows found in both. part.year % 5 == 0 is true for years that end in 0 or 5: we label those and the last year.

gaps = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "output_gaps_oecd.csv")
prices = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_annual.csv")
eo_loops = gaps.merge(prices, on=["iso3", "country", "year"])
eo_loops[eo_loops.country == "United Kingdom"].head(3)
iso3 country year output_gap inflation
1362 GBR United Kingdom 1985 -0.059 6.071
1363 GBR United Kingdom 1986 0.442 3.428
1364 GBR United Kingdom 1987 3.132 4.149 
def oecd_loops_chart(country="United States"):
    """Figure 13.17, extended: annual (output gap, inflation) points of one country, OECD estimates of the gap."""
    part = eo_loops[eo_loops.country == country]
    label = part.year.astype(str).where((part.year % 5 == 0) | (part.year == part.year.max()), "")
    x_range = [np.floor(part.output_gap.min()) - 1, np.ceil(part.output_gap.max()) + 1]
    y_range = [np.floor(min(part.inflation.min(), 0)) - 1, np.ceil(part.inflation.max()) + 1]
    fig = px.line(part.assign(label=label), x="output_gap", y="inflation", text="label", markers=True,
                  hover_name="year", title=f"{country}: inflation and the output gap, {part.year.min()}–{part.year.max()}",
                  labels={"output_gap": "Output gap, Ỹ (percent, OECD)", "inflation": "CPI inflation (percent)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2), marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=7), textposition="top center")
    fig.update_layout(xaxis=dict(range=x_range, zeroline=True), yaxis=dict(range=y_range))
    return fig
interact(oecd_loops_chart, country=Dropdown(options=sorted(eo_loops.country.unique()), value="United States",
                                            description="country", style=WIDE));

  • Choose the United Kingdom: a textbook loop. The boom of 1987–1989 (output 5.7 percent above potential in 1988) raised inflation to 8.0 percent in 1990; the recession that followed (−4.1 percent in 1993) brought it down to 2.6 percent. Sweden shows a similar loop in the same years.

Figure 18: Forecasting and the Great Recession

Goal. See how professional forecasters missed the Great Recession, quarter after quarter.

If economists understand fluctuations so well, can they forecast them? The Survey of Professional Forecasters, run by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, asks experts every quarter for their forecast of U.S. employment. This figure stays U.S.-only: the survey covers only the U.S. economy, and the similar survey of the European Central Bank asks about growth, inflation and unemployment rates, not about the number of jobs. The economists James Stock and Mark Watson called this figure “the mother of all forecast errors”.

Python note. melt stacks columns into rows: id_vars="date" stays a column, and the names of the other columns go into a new column series. .map(NAMES) replaces each column name by its readable name from the dictionary. spf.columns[2:] is the list of column names from the third one on (the forecasts). column[4:8] takes characters 4 to 7 of a text, here the year, and column[-1] its last character, here the quarter.

What to notice.

BOOK_FOUR = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Euro area", "Japan")


def oecd_chart(countries=BOOK_FOUR):
    """Figure 13.19: annual CPI inflation in the chosen economies since 1960."""
    part = prices[prices.country.isin(countries)]
    low, high, ticks = -3, 26, [0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25]
    for wider_low, wider_high in [(-10, 60), (-20, 120)]:     # a wider axis only when a chosen country needs it
        if part.inflation.min() < low or part.inflation.max() > high:
            low, high, ticks = wider_low, wider_high, None
    title = "Inflation was high everywhere in the 1970s and low after the 1980s"
    if set(countries) != set(BOOK_FOUR):
        title = "CPI inflation, percent a year" + missing_or_off(part, "inflation", countries, low, high)
    fig = px.line(part, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(countries)}, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=2.5)
    fig.update_layout(xaxis=dict(range=[1958, 2027], tickvals=[1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020]),  # no 1960 next to 0
                      yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=ticks),
                      legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"), legend_title_text="")
    return fig

# Your turn: try it here

Figure 20: Costless disinflation by coordinating expectations

Goal. See how a credible central bank could lower inflation without a recession.

So far firms expected last year’s inflation (adaptive expectations). Under rational expectations, an idea developed by Robert Lucas, people use all the information they have, including the central bank’s announced target. The AS curve then uses expected inflation \(\pi^e_t\) instead of \(\pi_{t-1}\):

\[\pi_t = \pi^e_t + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}. \qquad (13.6)\]

The Fed announces a cut in its target from 4 to 2 percent. If firms believe it and expect 2 percent, the AS curve moves down together with the AD curve, and the economy goes straight from \(A\) to \(B\) with output at potential. To see the middle ground, the slider sets the credibility of the announcement: the share of the cut that firms build into their expectations, \(\pi^e = \text{credibility} \times \bar{\pi}' + (1 - \text{credibility}) \times 4\). Credibility 0 is the adaptive case of Figure 10.

def credible_disinflation(credibility=1.0, pi_new=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Figure 13.20: the target falls from PI_OLD to pi_new; expectations follow it in proportion to credibility."""
    pi_e = credibility * pi_new + (1 - credibility) * PI_OLD
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, pi_bar=pi_new, m=m, nu=nu)
    fig = asad_figure()
    old_as, old_ad = "AS", "AD"
    if abs(pi_e - PI_OLD) < 0.6 * max(1, nu):          # no label when it would sit on the label of AS′
        old_as = ""
    if abs(pi_new - PI_OLD) * min(1, B_BAR * m) < 0.6:  # ... or on the label of AD′
        old_ad = ""
    if pi_e != PI_OLD:
        add_as(fig, old_as, GRAY, PI_OLD, nu, dash="dash")
    add_ad(fig, old_ad, GRAY, pi_bar=PI_OLD, m=m, dash="dash")
    add_as(fig, "AS′", TEAL, pi_e, nu)
    add_ad(fig, "AD′", BLUE, pi_bar=pi_new, m=m)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, PI_OLD, "A")
    add_point(fig, Y, pi, "B")
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, PI_OLD, Y, pi)
    asad_axes(fig, f"Credibility {credibility:.2f}: expected π = {pi_e:.2f}% → π = {pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {Y:.2f}%")
    return fig
interact(credible_disinflation,
         credibility=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.0, max=1.0, step=0.25, description="credibility of the new target",
                                 style=WIDE),
         pi_new=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="new target π̄′ (%)", style=WIDE),
         m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
         nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25, description="AS slope ν̄", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Figure 20 with a precomputed slider for credibility
slider_figure(credible_disinflation, "credibility", [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0], start=1.0,
              label="credibility of the new target")

Source. Adapted from Figure 13.20 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed., W. W. Norton. Our own interactive version, with our own parameter values, layout and code; it is not a copy of the original figure. The credibility slider, which spans the cases between adaptive and fully credible expectations, is our addition.

What to notice.

  • With full credibility, inflation falls to 2 percent at once and output stays at potential: a costless disinflation.
  • With credibility 0, we are back in Figure 10: inflation falls only to 3 percent and output to −1 percent.
  • In between, every bit of credibility saves output. This is why central banks explain their policy, announce inflation targets, and build a reputation: managing expectations is one of the main tools of modern monetary policy. It also explains the time consistency problem: a central bank that might later be tempted to inflate cannot be fully believed, so a commitment to a rule (like Ulysses tied to the mast) can be worth more than discretion.

Key numbers: the cost of a disinflation

We compare the total output lost while inflation falls from 4 to 2 percent, under adaptive expectations (the whole path of Figure 11) and with a fully credible announcement.

adaptive = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, 2.0)
Y_credible, pi_credible = solve_asad(2.0, pi_bar=2.0)
print(f"Adaptive expectations: output lost over {T_MAX} periods = {-adaptive.Y.sum():.2f}% of potential output")
print(f"Fully credible target: period-1 output = {Y_credible:.2f}%, inflation = {pi_credible:.2f}%")
Adaptive expectations: output lost over 20 periods = 2.00% of potential output
Fully credible target: period-1 output = 0.00%, inflation = 2.00%

Under adaptive expectations the disinflation costs about 2 percent of a year’s output; with full credibility it costs nothing. The Lucas critique makes the general point: a model with fixed expectations can give wrong answers about a new policy, because people change their expectations when the policy changes.

Your turn. What output does period 1 bring with credibility 0.5? How much of the adaptive recession does half credibility avoid?

Hint

Expected inflation is 0.5 * 2.0 + 0.5 * 4.0; pass it to solve_asad(..., pi_bar=2.0).
