Other countries since 1871

Long price series exist for other rich countries too. The Jordà–Schularick–Taylor Macrohistory Database has consumer prices for 17 more countries from 1870 to 2020; we extend them to 2025 with the World Bank’s inflation rates. The file inflation_long_annual.csv has one row per country and year (for the United Kingdom, the series used above, from 1737). We cut each country’s years into the same 20-year windows as above and compute the mean and the standard deviation of each window. For the United Kingdom this gives exactly the points of the chart above.

Python note. // divides and drops the remainder, so (year - 1737) // 20 * 20 + 1737 is the first year of the 20-year window that contains year (1990 gives 1977). .agg(["mean", "std", "count"]) computes three numbers for each group, and reset_index() turns the group labels back into columns.

history = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_long_annual.csv")
history["start"] = (history.year - 1737) // 20 * 20 + 1737            # first year of the 20-year window
windows = history.groupby(["country", "start"]).inflation.agg(["mean", "std", "count"]).reset_index()
windows = windows[(windows["count"] == 20) | (windows.start == 2017)]  # full windows and the latest, partial one
windows["period"] = windows.start.astype(str) + "–" + (windows.start + windows["count"] - 1).astype(str)
windows["distance"] = np.sqrt((windows["mean"] - 2) ** 2 + windows["std"] ** 2)
windows[windows.country == "United Kingdom"].tail(3).round(2)
country start mean std count period distance
153 United Kingdom 1977 6.34 4.07 20 1977–1996 5.95
154 United Kingdom 1997 1.92 1.06 20 1997–2016 1.07
155 United Kingdom 2017 3.63 2.70 9 2017–2025 3.16

Look at your data. Two windows are wildly off the chart. In Germany, prices rose about a billion-fold in 1923 alone, so the average inflation of 1917–1936 is billions of percent. Japan’s 1937–1956 window holds the war and the inflation that followed it (an average of 71 percent a year). Averages of yearly rates are fragile when one year is extreme: the chart counts such windows in its title instead of drawing them.

def windows_chart(countries=("United Kingdom",)):
    """Figure 13.21, extended: average and volatility of inflation in 20-year windows, chosen countries."""
    part = windows[windows.country.isin(countries)]
    x_range, y_range = [-3, 8.5], [-0.7, 13]
    if part["mean"].max() > 8.5 or part["std"].max() > 13 or part["mean"].min() < -3:
        x_range, y_range = [-5, 40], [-3, 80]           # one wider view, only when a chosen country needs it
    off = part[(part["mean"] > x_range[1]) | (part["std"] > y_range[1])]
    title = "No data for this choice"
    if len(part) > 0:
        best = part.loc[part.distance.idxmin()]
        title = f"Closest to the goal: {best.country} {best.period} (distance {best.distance:.2f})"
    if len(off) > 0:
        title += f"; {len(off)} off the chart"
    fig = px.scatter(part, x="mean", y="std", color="country", hover_name="period",
                     color_discrete_map=INFLATION_COLORS, hover_data={"distance": ":.2f", "count": True}, title=title,
                     labels={"mean": "Average inflation (percent)", "std": "Volatility of inflation (percent)",
                             "country": "Country", "count": "years"})
    fig.update_traces(marker_size=11)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[2], y=[0], mode="markers", name="Goal", marker=dict(color="black", size=14, symbol="star")))
    fig.update_layout(xaxis_range=x_range, yaxis_range=y_range, legend_title_text="")
    return fig
interact(windows_chart, countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(windows.country.unique()), value=["United Kingdom"],
                                                 rows=8, description="countries", style=WIDE));

On the website, all 18 countries are in the legend: click a country to add it, and double-click the chart to rescale the axes.

  • Add the other countries: in 16 of the 18, the window closest to the goal is 1997–2016, the years of inflation targets and independent central banks. Canada’s is even closer than the U.K.’s (1.86 percent average inflation with a volatility of 0.68). In Japan and Switzerland, where inflation averaged close to zero in 1997–2016 (0.1 and 0.5 percent), the partial window 2017–2025 comes closest.
  • The war years were volatile everywhere: Finland’s 1917–1936 window has a volatility of 57 points.

Summary

  • A monetary policy rule \(R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\) turns the IS curve into the downward-sloping AD curve \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\); the Phillips curve is the upward-sloping AS curve. Their crossing gives this period’s output and inflation; the steady state has inflation on target and output at potential.
  • Because expected inflation is sticky, every shock is followed by slow transition dynamics: an inflation shock brings stagflation, a lower target costs a recession, and a temporary demand boom must be paid for with a later recession. The economy moves in counterclockwise loops, and the U.S. data show them too.
  • A simple rule with Taylor’s numbers tracks the fed funds rate surprisingly well, with large gaps in the 1970s, after 2008 and in 2021–2022. Data revisions can change what the numbers say.
  • Expectations are central: a credible target can lower inflation at little cost, which is why modern central banks adopt inflation targets and value their reputation.
  • The next chapter turns to financial crises and how they fit into the short-run model.
